days.title: Cell Membrane Structure
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the fluid mosaic model of the membrane.
  • Identify the components of the membrane.
  • Explain the functions of each component.
  • Relate structure to selective permeability.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Fluid mosaic model — describes membrane as a fluid bilayer with embedded proteins.
  • Phospholipid bilayer — two layers of phospholipids.
  • Amphipathic — having both hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions.

📚 Lesson Content

A. The Fluid Mosaic Model

Proposed by Singer and Nicolson (1972). The membrane is a dynamic structure — phospholipids and proteins move laterally.

B. Components

ComponentFunction
PhospholipidsForm the bilayer barrier
Integral proteinsTransport, channels, receptors
Peripheral proteinsSignaling, structural support
CholesterolRegulates fluidity
Glycolipids/GlycoproteinsCell recognition, adhesion

C. Selective Permeability

The membrane allows some substances to pass but blocks others. Small nonpolar molecules (O₂, CO₂) cross easily; ions and large polar molecules need transport proteins.

scenarios.text: Forms the basic barrier of the membrane.
Helps the membrane stay fluid at low temperatures.
Acts as a channel for ions.
Identifies the cell as 'self'.
Sits on the inner or outer surface, not embedded.
O₂ crosses the membrane freely.

questions.text: Which model describes the membrane as a fluid structure with embedded proteins?
What is the role of cholesterol in the membrane?
Which part of the phospholipid is hydrophobic?

takeaways: The plasma membrane follows the fluid mosaic model.
Phospholipids form the bilayer; proteins perform transport and signaling.
Selective permeability is the key feature of the membrane.

days.title: Passive Transport & Osmosis
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate diffusion, osmosis, and facilitated diffusion.
  • Explain how concentration gradients drive passive transport.
  • Predict the effect of tonicity on cells.
  • Relate passive transport to real-life examples.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Diffusion — movement of molecules from high to low concentration.
  • Osmosis — diffusion of water across a semipermeable membrane.
  • Facilitated diffusion — passive transport using a protein channel.
  • Tonicity — relative solute concentration of a solution.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Passive Transport Types

TypeDescriptionEnergy?
Simple diffusionSmall nonpolar molecules pass directlyNo
Facilitated diffusionUses a channel/carrier proteinNo
OsmosisWater moves through a semipermeable membraneNo

B. Tonicity

  • Isotonic — equal solute; cell stays the same.
  • Hypertonic — higher solute outside; cell shrinks (crenation).
  • Hypotonic — lower solute outside; cell swells (may lyse).

C. Real-Life Examples

  • Water absorbed by plant roots (osmosis)
  • Oxygen entering red blood cells (diffusion)
  • Glucose entering cells via GLUT transporters (facilitated diffusion)

pairs.right: Uses a protein channel, no ATP

scenarios.text: A red blood cell in pure water swells and bursts.
A plant wilts in saltwater.
A cell stays the same size in a solution.
Water moves into a plant root hair.
Oxygen enters a cell without a protein.
Glucose enters via GLUT protein.

questions.text: Which of the following does NOT require ATP?
A cell in a hypertonic solution will:
Facilitated diffusion differs from simple diffusion because it:

takeaways: Passive transport moves substances down a concentration gradient without ATP.
Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a semipermeable membrane.
Tonicity determines whether a cell swells, shrinks, or stays the same.
Facilitated diffusion uses proteins but no energy.

days.title: Active Transport
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Explain what active transport is.
  • Describe the sodium-potassium pump.
  • Differentiate primary from secondary active transport.
  • Relate active transport to real-life applications.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Active transport — movement against the concentration gradient using ATP.
  • Sodium-potassium pump — 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in per ATP.
  • Primary active transport — directly uses ATP.
  • Secondary active transport — uses the gradient created by primary transport.

📚 Lesson Content

A. What Is Active Transport?

Moves molecules against their concentration gradient — from low to high concentration. Requires energy (ATP).

B. The Sodium-Potassium Pump

  • Pumps 3 Na⁺ OUT of the cell
  • Pumps 2 K⁺ INTO the cell
  • Uses 1 ATP per cycle
  • Maintains resting membrane potential in nerve cells

C. Why It Matters

  • Nerve impulse transmission
  • Muscle contraction
  • Nutrient uptake in the intestine
  • Kidney function (reabsorbing nutrients)

scenarios.text: A molecule moves from low to high concentration.
3 Na⁺ exit the cell while 2 K⁺ enter.
Cell uses ATP directly for transport.
A nerve cell maintains its resting potential.
Glucose is absorbed in the intestine against its gradient.
A cell uses a Na⁺ gradient to move another molecule.

questions.text: What does active transport require that passive transport does not?
How many Na⁺ ions does the Na⁺/K⁺ pump move per ATP?
Which process relies on the Na⁺/K⁺ pump?

takeaways: Active transport moves substances against their gradient using ATP.
The Na⁺/K⁺ pump is essential for nerve function.
Primary active transport uses ATP directly; secondary uses a gradient.
Active transport is critical for nutrient uptake and cell signaling.

days.title: Endocytosis & Exocytosis
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate endocytosis from exocytosis.
  • Distinguish phagocytosis from pinocytosis.
  • Describe receptor-mediated endocytosis.
  • Give real-life examples of bulk transport.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Endocytosis — cell takes in material via vesicles.
  • Exocytosis — cell releases material via vesicles.
  • Phagocytosis — cell engulfs large particles (cell eating).
  • Pinocytosis — cell takes in fluids (cell drinking).

📚 Lesson Content

A. Endocytosis — Three Types

TypeWhat It Takes InExample
PhagocytosisLarge particles/cellsWBC engulfing bacteria
PinocytosisFluids & small solutesIntestinal cells
Receptor-mediatedSpecific moleculesCholesterol uptake via LDL receptors

B. Exocytosis

Vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane and release contents outside.

  • Neurotransmitter release
  • Hormone secretion (insulin)
  • Mucus release
  • Waste removal

scenarios.text: A white blood cell engulfs a bacterium.
A cell takes in extracellular fluid.
Insulin is released from a pancreatic cell.
Cholesterol is taken in via LDL receptors.
A neuron releases neurotransmitters.
A cell expels waste through vesicles.

questions.text: What is the difference between endocytosis and exocytosis?
Which process involves engulfing large particles?
Which of the following is an example of exocytosis?

takeaways: Endocytosis brings material IN; exocytosis releases material OUT.
Phagocytosis = cell eating; pinocytosis = cell drinking.
Exocytosis is essential for secretion and waste removal.
